principles.text: A pullback that doesn't even touch the 9 EMA, while holding a prior breakout gap, is a sign of immense underlying strength.
Uses the 9 EMA as the objective level/guide for deciding whether to stay in or exit volatile (e.g. crypto) positions.
The number of positions held is irrelevant on its own -- what matters is market breadth, individual stock action, and the indices, not a fixed position count.
Don't try to outsmart or second-guess the market -- in a strong market, price can run much further than expected; let the market signal when it no longer wants to go up.
Avoid names where volume is too low relative to market cap -- expect a wide spread in the first 5-15 minutes of trading on such names.
Whether to require taking out the opening-range high on the 1-minute vs. 5-minute chart depends on where the market opens and how extended it is intraday.
When a stock approaches a declining resistance moving average (e.g. the 50 EMA), watch how price reacts there -- no rejection and a clean push through is a sign of strength.
Don't rely on charts alone -- line up the market, the sector, and the individual stock's context/rationale together; being obsessed with the chart in isolation loses a big part of the edge.
Index/sector context matters a lot for timing entries and improving win rate, but it isn't 'all about' the index -- individual stock selection and pattern still matter a great deal.
When comparing two similar names in the same group, prefer the relatively stronger one (e.g. choosing MU over SNDK).
Core trading philosophy: focus on getting entries with the tightest possible risk right before a range expansion.
Getting stopped out repeatedly (washed out) on the same names is a signal to go back and study whether entries or stop placement need improvement.

How much to trim into an earnings gap-risk event should be sized to the adverse gap you can psychologically/financially accept -- the more profit cushion, the less you need to trim; it's never wrong to book some profit.
Overexposure is subjective -- it's defined by what the individual trader can personally tolerate losing, not by an external rule on position count.

Build pattern recognition by studying past trades (especially shakeout entries) for real hours of work; if it still doesn't click after genuine effort, that entry style may simply not be a fit -- and that's fine.

Pick the breakout timeframe (1-minute vs. 5-minute vs. 15-minute) based on the stop size it implies -- a wider range on a longer timeframe means a wider percentage stop, so use a finer timeframe to keep risk tight.
